title: Conversion (CCC 1427–1433)
hookLine: conversion is a lifelong turning of the heart

lines: THE LORD TURNING LOOKED ON PETER.
cards: A courtyard at night, a fire, a servant girl staring. Peter has said it three times now: he doesn't know the man. Somewhere a cock crows.

Then comes a line in Luke's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, so short it's easy to read past: "And the Lord turning looked on Peter." Peter remembers what Jesus told him, goes outside, and weeps bitterly.
This wasn't his first day as a disciple; he'd left his boats long before. And still, here, he turns again.

teach.b: Day sixty-two told this night as a story; today, the Catechism's word for it: conversion.
Mark's Gospel opens Jesus's preaching with it, in the Douay-Rheims: "The time is accomplished, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent, and believe the gospel."
That call comes first to people who don't yet know Christ, the Catechism says, and the first, deep conversion happens in baptism. But it doesn't end there.

It speaks of a second conversion, an uninterrupted task for the whole Church, which, quoting the Second Vatican Council, it calls holy and always in need of purification. So conversion isn't a moment you get through once.
It's a direction. And it isn't mainly a human effort. It's the movement of a contrite heart, drawn and moved by grace to answer God's merciful love.
Peter is the picture: after three denials, a look of infinite mercy draws tears of repentance from him.
Joel, in the Douay-Rheims: "rend your hearts, and not your garments."

teach.h: EVEN THE TURNING IS A GIFT.
teach.b: The call is first to an interior turning, not outward works like sackcloth and ashes, though without a change of heart those works would be empty, and with one they follow.

It's a reorientation of the whole life: away from evil, toward God, with real sorrow and the hope of mercy. And the Catechism is honest that the human heart is heavy and hard, so God has to give a new one.

teach.h: CONVERT US, O LORD, TO THEE.
teach.b: It quotes Lamentations: "Convert us, O Lord, to thee, and we shall be converted." Even the turning is a gift.

how: Catholics speak of daily conversion and mark it in the examination of conscience, the penitential act at the start of Mass, Lent, and the sacrament of reconciliation.

games.q: you're Peter. you've just denied him a third time, and across the courtyard Jesus turns and looks at you. what happens next in Luke?
o: you deny him a fourth time.
you go out and weep bitterly.
you run to him and apologize.
games.why: Peter remembered the word of the Lord, went out and wept bitterly. the Catechism calls that look one of infinite mercy.

practice: Let one small thing come to mind that's been pointing the wrong way: a habit of sharpness with one person, a lie that makes life easier, a grudge you're feeding.
Picture yourself turning to face the other way, the way you'd turn your whole body toward someone who called your name.
If you pray, ask God for that turn, with the words of Lamentations or in silence; if you don't, just hold the image of turning.

wordCard.voice: Conversion. A turning of the whole heart toward God, begun in baptism, never finished, and itself a gift of grace. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: the New Testament noun rendered 'repentance'; Mark 1:15 uses its verb.

carryVoice: Your line: keep turning. Peter turned, and then kept turning, for the rest of the story. Same time tomorrow.
